The protested merchandise consists of cordless leaf blowers used for home and light commercial applications. The blowers generate a supercharged airflow that can go from 0 to 157 mph in one second and produce over 600 CFM of air volume. The protestant explains that the leaf blowers were manufactured by an unrelated supplier, Greenworks (Vietnam) Company Limited (“Greenworks”) at several plants in 
2 Vietnam. Prior to sourcing the leaf blowers from Greenworks’ production facilities in Vietnam, the Protestant sourced the merchandise from a facility in China. The Protestant avers that beginning in November 2020, production was completely and permanently transitioned to Greenworks’ production facility in Vietnam. In support of its claims, the Protestant submitted production videos, entry documents and a bill of materials. The Protestant also submitted a statement from Greenworks attesting to the manufacturing transition and identifying the initial shipments of leaf blowers that were exported from the plant in Vietnam. The key manufacturing processes to produce the leaf blowers in Vietnam include production of the injection molded housings and blower tube nozzle, production of the motor (including the rotor and stator subassemblies), electrical wiring, and final assembly of the finished leaf blower, each described in further detail below. However, we note that according to the bill of materials, the printed circuit board assembly (“PCBA”) used to produce the subject leaf blower was sourced from China. Injection Molded Housings In support of its claim that the injection molded housings were manufactured in Vietnam, the Protestant submitted a video produced by Greenworks, which shows their plastic injection molding site and identifies the production lines used to mold the leaf blower components, all occurring at the supplier’s facility within an industrial park in Vietnam. Motor Production The Protestant submitted videos and a bill of materials in support of its claim that motor production, including manufacture of the rotor and stator from Chinese origin components, occurred in Vietnam. 1. Rotor Subassembly The Protestant states that the rotor subassembly was manufactured in Vietnam using the following components of Chinese origin: core lamination, magnets, stainless steel sleeve, rotor shaft, front and rear insulating sleeves, spring, and rotating disk. In Vietnam, the shaft was first machine pressed into a retaining ring that holds the rotor components in place. This was followed by gluing and pressing the lamination stack and permanent magnets onto the shaft and retaining assembly. Subsequently, the bearing and rotor housing were pressed onto the shaft and magnet assembly to form the rotor subassembly. 2. Stator Subassembly The stator subassembly was also manufactured in Vietnam using mostly Chinese origin components, including the following: slot insulation paper, slot wedge, wires, core lamination, copper strip, terminal, insulating varnish, and dual-wall heat shrink tubes. In 
3 Vietnam, the stator core was first pressed into a plastic stator housing. The stator core and plastic housing were then placed into a winding machine where they were wound with enameled copper wire from Vietnam. These coiled armatures were then pressed through another machine where they were joined to the stator housing while the lamination stack was secured to the outside of the stator subassembly. 3. Final Motor Assembly The rotor and stator subassemblies were connected manually by fitting the rotor shaft into the stator housing and pressing the two subassemblies together. Then, the entire assembly was fit into a motor housing, and the components were screwed into place. The rotor cap, which controls the fan’s movement, was then pressed into place and the motor was tested for quality and functionality. Electrical Wiring and Final Assembly of the Leaf Blower During the next phase of production in Vietnam, the electrical connections were soldered together with the fan and placed into the plastic fan housing. Next, the Chinese-origin PCBA and the electrical switching components were connected to the motor and fan subassembly. All of these components were then fitted into the plastic blower housing and the electrical wiring was fitted into place. Lastly, the plastic housing was screwed into place to cover all of the functional components, resulting in the main leaf blower unit. This was followed by testing and packaging with the plastic tube nozzle that was produced in Vietnam.1 The Protestant explains that the entire production process requires over 60 individual workstations across multiple factory floors and production lines, involving between 57-76 workers, including 18-25 specially trained, skilled workers that manage the motor production, injection molding, electrical circuitry and safety at the production site in Vietnam. Producing each leaf blower unit takes approximately 60 minutes to complete. The protested merchandise consists of 15 entries of leaf blowers that were entered between December 22, 2020, through June 4, 2021. The Customs Form (“CF”) 7501 identified the country of origin of the protested merchandise as China. We note that while the Protestant’s submission refers to Greenworks as the Protestant’s supplier, the original invoices submitted with the protest commercial invoices were issued by a company called “HongKong Sun Rise Trading Limited” (“HKSR”), with the name and address of a manufacturer located in China, identified as Changzhou Globe Co., Ltd. (“Changzhou”). The accompanying commercial invoices also identified the country of origin of the protested merchandise as China. The Protestant stated in their protest submission that “revised commercial invoices with the corrected country of origin for all 1 Some entries are imported with a battery sourced from Vietnam and a charger sourced from China, both of which are packed separately. 
4 of the entries impacted by this issue are available, if necessary, upon request from CBP.”

In your letter dated July 27, 2026, on behalf of your client, Hesai (Thailand) Limited, you requested a country of origin ruling on a Light Detection and Ranging (LiDAR) Module. Descriptive literature was provided for our review. The item under consideration is described as the Hesai OT128 LiDAR Module, which functions as a high-resolution, 360-degree automotive sensor for autonomous driving and smart logistics. The module creates detailed 3-dimensional maps for obstacle detection, navigation, and environmental awareness by using laser beams to measure distances. It provides core perception capabilities for L4 autonomous driving (robotaxis/robot trucks) and is applied to industrial automation scenarios such as smart ports, automated guided vehicles (AGVs), Autonomous Mobile Robots (AMRs), and service robots to enable precise navigation and obstacle avoidance. The OT128 LiDAR Module is composed of a Top Cover, Cover Lens, Lens Housing (also referred to as the opto-mechanical unit), and Base. The Lens Housing consists of the Lens Housing Semi-Finished Product (SFP), which includes the RX Module, TX Module, a series of lenses, the Top Main Board (TMB) Semi-Finished Product (this includes the TMB Board), and the Heat Sink Semi-Finished Product. Core components of the Lens Housing SFP include the RX Module, TX Module, and a series of lenses. The TX Module is responsible for generating and sending out pulses of laser light into the environment. The TX Module includes the Transmitter Board, flexible printed circuit boards (FPC), front and back brackets, and a stop aperture. The RX Module is responsible for detecting the reflected light and enabling distance calculation. It includes the Receiver Front Board and Receiver Back Board, FPCs, a stop aperture, and a filter. The TMB SFP contains the Top Main Board PCBA, which controls the timing of laser emission and reception. Additionally, this PCBA collects analog-to-digital converter (ADC) waveforms and calculates distance and reflectance. The resulting packetized point cloud data is then sent to the Bottom Main Board (BMB) located in the Base. The TMB SFP also includes an optical communication transmitter board of Chinese origin. 

The BMB is part of the Base SFP and controls the wireless power supply module to power the optical engine, controls the rotation of the motor, collects encoder data to obtain real-time angle information, repackages the real-time point cloud data obtained from TMB, and then transmits it externally via the Ethernet. In your letter, you provide two manufacturing scenarios. The difference between scenarios is the country in which certain PCBAs undergo surface mount technology (SMT) assembly; all other assembly processes remain the same. Final assembly of the LiDAR Module occurs in Thailand in both scenarios. In scenario I, the TMB PCBA and BMB PCBA are assembled in Vietnam using standard SMT processes. The RX PCBA and TX PCBA are assembled in China using standard SMT processes and sent to Thailand for assembly into the RX and TX modules. Subsequent assembly processes and programming are completed in Thailand, and the finished product is shipped from Thailand to the United States. In scenario II, the TMB PCBA, BMB PCBA, and RX PCBA (RBB and RFB) are assembled in Vietnam using standard SMT processes. All other components of the finished product, including the TX PCBA, are of Chinese origin. The PCBAs and all other components are sent to Thailand where subsequent assembly processes and programming are completed, and the finished product is shipped from Thailand to the United States. Other than the changes in the manufacturing location for the various printed circuit boards, the assembly process of the LiDAR module occurs in Thailand. This process is predominantly a simple multi-stage assembly where components are combined, fastened, snapped, and bonded into place. The assembly consists of five stations. The automated station handles material loading and unloading, runs automated equipment, and disposes of products via prompts. The manual bonding station identifies adhesives, uses proper dispensing tools, and performs bonding and mounting. The manual fastening station identifies the correct screws, uses calibrated torque wrenches, and fastens screws. The manual station performs basic simple manual operations including loading, wiping, and handling. Finally, the quality inspection station conducts 100 percent inspection of products using specified tools. Various curing steps and testing steps are also completed once the module is fully assembled.

In your letter dated August 25, 2026, you requested a country of origin ruling on pressure washer nozzles, foam cannons, and guns. Descriptive literature was provided for our review. The first item under consideration is described as a 5-piece pressure washer nozzle tip set (SKU T03-NK2). The set consists of five color-coded 1/4-inch quick-connect nozzles tips. The tips are used with pressure washer guns to provide multiple spray patterns for different cleaning scenarios. The red has a 0° angle for a concentrated jet, the yellow has a 15° angle for tough grime, the green has a 25° angle for general-purpose use, the white has a 40° angle for vehicles and delicate surfaces, and the black has a 65° angle for low-pressure soap application. Each nozzle tip comprises a plastic cap, a nozzle insert (stainless steel for red, green, yellow, and white tips and no separate insert for the black), and a nozzle body (stainless steel for red, green, yellow and white tips, and brass for the black). The second item under consideration is described as a foam cannon kit (SKU S02-A02K), which is a heavy-duty car wash sprayer designed for high-pressure application. The unit features a side-filling port and an integrated measuring cup, which facilitate precise soap dispensing and mitigate the risk of spillage. The 1-liter reservoir is manufactured with a reinforced, wide-neck design to enhance structural integrity against high-frequency vibrations. The primary assembly consists of an aluminum alloy and stainless-steel nozzle, equipped with a standard 1/4-inch quick-connect fitting. The configuration is said to provide corrosion resistance, adjustable spray patterns, and compatibility with a wide range of pressure washer systems. The third item under consideration is described as the foam cannon kit with soft-grip short pressure washer gun (SKU S02-A02K2). The kit is the same as the second item but also includes a brass adapter and the gun described in item four. The kit is designed for high-pressure cleaning applications, emphasizing compact dimensions and maneuverability. The spray gun features a soft-grip handle engineered to reduce operator
fatigue during prolonged use. The kit includes a solid brass adapter designed to facilitate a secure, leak-resistant connection to standard pressure washer hoses. The short-profile design of the spray gun is intended to enhance control and accessibility in confined areas, such as vehicle wheel wells and engine compartments. The fourth item under consideration is described as a short pressure washer gun with rigid plastic handle (SKU P01-XQ06). The device is manufactured for high-pressure cleaning applications, specifically designed to enhance maneuverability in confined spaces such as wheel wells, undercarriages, and engine compartments. The gun features a rigid, high-impact plastic handle designed for ergonomic use and durability in both professional and residential environments. The internal valve assembly is constructed of solid brass and stainless steel, intended to ensure structural integrity, corrosion resistance, and the reliable management of high-pressure water flow. The nozzle tips, foam cannons and guns are made with components sourced from China and Malaysia. The Chinese components include the stainless-steel (for the nozzle insert, nozzle body, inlet connector, foam generator core, extension tube, valve stem, and valve sleeve), plastic caps, 1-liter bottle, suction tube, adjustment knob, screws, nozzle sleeve pin, foam filter, spray blade holder, spray blades, nozzle housing, O-rings, red side cover, gun housing, trigger safety lock, trigger, valve spring, valve ball, valve seat seal, springs, retaining ring and locking balls. The Malaysian components including the brass bar stock used for the jet nozzle, bottle adapter, main valve body, adjustment valve nut, adjustment valve step, adjustment valve cap, brass nozzle, adapter body, high-pressure inlet connector, valve seat, valve core plug, valve sleeve, retaining nut, coupler body, and locking sleeve. All of the components are then sent to Malaysia where the pressure washer nozzles, foam cannons and guns are constructed by CNC machining the stainless-steel or brass, depending on the component, precision drilling the parts, and deburring to form the finished products. Once the metal components are made, they are then assembled with the remaining Chinese components to form the complete nozzles, foam cannons and guns. The nozzles, foam cannons and guns are then tested and packaged for retail sale. The five pressure washer tips in item one are placed in a clear blister plastic face, molded over a sturdy cardboard backing card. The foam cannon and tips in item two are placed in a white molded plastic insert before being placed in a sturdy retail box. The packaging for item three is the same as item two but includes additional spaces for the gun and adapter. The pressure washer gun in item four is placed in a clear blister plastic face, molded over a sturdy cardboard backing card.

The VR Headset System is a three-part, VR and mixed reality (“MR”) system that performs a suite of computing and data processing tasks, including executing applications for entertainment, media, and productivity purposes. The VR Headset System consists of the following three components: (1) The Headset, which is a head-mounted display (“HMD”) that contains lenses and serves as the display of the device. The Headset has user-facing sensors that track the hands, eyes, and face of the user; converts the user’s motions to signals and sends them to the below-described “Puck,” and receives and converts data from the Puck to display on the lenses; (2) The Puck, which conducts the main computing and data processing functions of the VR Headset System. The Puck’s components manage the computing, data processing, storage, graphics processing, WiFi/Bluetooth connectivity, power, and
thermal aspects of the system. It runs a [ ] OS that is pre-installed on the device and stores and executes a library of entertainment and social applications that are installed automatically upon the device set-up, as well as applications that users can create or download from third-party websites following a simple initial verification; and (3) A tether cable that connects the headset to the Puck. All three of the above components must be connected for the VR Headset System to function. The Headset is embedded with firmware that interacts exclusively with the Puck and cannot function independently of the Puck, even if physically connected to other devices. If connected solely to a tablet by a USB-C cable, the Headset could not control or transmit images for display on the tablet, or vice versa. The VR Headset System can be paired and used with standard peripheral devices for computers (e.g., a Bluetooth-enabled keyboard, mouse, gaming controllers, etc.). It can also be connected to separate computing and communications devices such as computers, phones, and gaming consoles, and, when so connected, these devices extend the display of media such as videos, photos, and text from the Headset. The Puck includes the following main components:  The main logic board (“MLB”) that stores applications, runs the OS, performs the computing and data processing functions of the VR Headset System, and executes the applications with which the user can interact through the Headset;  Between 1,100 and 1,200 MLB sub-components, including the following: o A Taiwanese-origin [ ] Chipset System-on-Chip (“SoC”), which is the main processing unit and contains a graphics processing unit that runs the applications and content with which a user interacts; o A Memory/Storage Chip from Korea, Taiwan, or China, which contains non- volatile storage for the OS, applications, and system resources;  One supporting printed circuit board assembly (“PCBA”), mounted with three switches and connectors that interact with the MLB to allow the user to trigger a reset of the device;  Wireless link radio frequency integrated circuits (“RFICs”) that wirelessly connect the Puck to a WiFi network, from which it can download new content and deliver that content to the Headset display. The Puck controls all wireless communications.  Battery and power management integrated circuits (“ICs”) that manage power delivery for the Puck to operate, including when it is disconnected from an external power source. In the Puck, the largest portion of the components’ cost comes from Taiwan, and the largest quantity of the components comes from China. Between 1,100 and 1,200 of the around 1,300 components in the Puck are mounted to the MLB by surface mount technology (“SMT”), which occurs in Vietnam. The most expensive component on the MLB is produced outside of China—namely the [ ] Chipset, which is manufactured in Taiwan. Chinese components account for over 25% of the total MLB components by cost. The components of the Headset include: 2
 Six PCBAs that aggregate inputs from user motions and audio to provide to the Puck for processing, manage sensors that communicate data to the Puck via tether, and receive data from the Puck to display to the user on the lenses;  Between 1,200 and 1,300 PCBA subcomponents and integrated circuits, including: o A Microcontroller Unit (“MCU”) that manages the data aggregation, timing of sensors, and communication of the sensor data from the Headset to the Puck; o Field programmable gate arrays (“FGPAs”), which are flexible integrated circuits that can be programmed and designed to device specifications; o Nordic Radio Frequency (“nRF”)/Bluetooth chips that support the low-power usage of Bluetooth applications; o Light emitting diode (“LED”) drivers that help power the device by converting incoming power as required for the output;  Display and Optical Modules and Lenses that collect data from the PCBAs to project images to the user.  Cameras and Depth Sensors that primarily conduct positional tracking and depth perception functions to allow the device to locate itself within a particular space;  Audio circuitry, including microphones that capture audio and audio transducers that collect data to provide the audio experience for the user via the System PCBAs. In the Headset, the largest portion of both the components’ cost and quantity comes from China. Between 1,200 and 1,300 of the over 1,400 components in the Headset are mounted to the six supporting PCBAs by means of SMT in Vietnam. Other major components, including the display and lenses of the Headset, the camera and depth sensors, and the audio circuitry, allow users to access the content and data generated by the MLB and supported by the seven supporting PCBAs. Together, the system PCBAs account for a majority of the total BOM components by quantity. The tether cable/interconnect is an optical cable that converts electrical signals to fiber and back. The tether connects the Puck and the Headset, and, without the tether, neither component could function. The manufacturing steps for the VR Headset System will occur in four main stages: (1) the production of 2,700 to 2,800 components individual components in 10 different countries including Vietnam, China, Taiwan, the Philippines, Korea, Japan, Singapore, Malaysia, the United States, and Austria ; (2) production of the VR Headset System’s main PCBA (the MLB)—which is in the Puck—in Vietnam by means of SMT, software download and testing of the PCBAs; (3) production of seven Supporting PCBAs in Vietnam by means of SMT, software download, and testing of the PCBAs; and (4) final assembly, final software downloads, testing of the Headset and Puck and packout (“FATP”) of the VR Headset System in China. SMT of the MLB in Vietnam involves incorporating between 1,100 and 1,200 electrical components onto both sides of a bare PCB. Meta states that the MLB executes the computing, data and graphics processing, connectivity, and sensor integration and, therefore, this process creates the “brain” of the VR Headset System. The largest portion of the MLB’s components’ 3
quantity comes from Taiwan, and the largest portion of the supporting PCBA’s components come from Japan. SMT of the MLB requires several weeks of on-line manufacturing training for workers. SMT of the MLB line cycle takes over four hours to complete, with a total direct labor requirement of over 20 on-line operators. The importer states that, with few deviations, the SMT processes for the seven supporting PCBAs are similar to the SMT process for the MLB described above. After SMT, the eight Vietnamese-origin PCBAs will be shipped to China for FATP. For the Puck, FATP involves snapping, pasting, bending, and screwing the Puck sub-components and components together. The importer states that this process takes less than 8 minutes, a majority of the assembly is automated, and that none of the steps involved in the Puck FATP will alter the characteristics of the MLB that emerge from SMT in Vietnam. FATP of the Headset takes less than an hour of assembly time, though glue curing time takes significantly longer. FATP of the Headset includes assembly of the camera module, outer frame, optical module, left temple module, right temple module, membrane module, main line assembly, and main line test validation. The importer states that the steps involved in the Headset FATP will not alter the characteristics of the seven supporting PCBAs that emerge from SMT in Vietnam.

input.facts: In your letter dated September 2, 2026, you requested a country of origin ruling on a steering knuckle. The article under consideration is an automotive steering knuckle, identified as model number 10801126JT. The steering knuckle is a structural component of a vehicle's steering and suspension systems, serving as a load-bearing link between the wheel assembly and the chassis. It facilitates wheel support, positioning, and steering. It also withstands the steering forces, braking forces, lateral forces, and road-induced impact loads generated during vehicle operation. The steering knuckle consists of a steering knuckle body manufactured in Thailand and three bushings manufactured in China. In Thailand, the steering knuckle body undergoes multiple manufacturing and finishing operations, including shot blasting, grinding, electrophoretic coating, and precision machining. The machining operations include matching the bearing mounting bore, precision machining of key mounting and functional surfaces, and machining the mounting holes for the dust shield. These operations establish the dimensions and functional surfaces necessary for the steering knuckle body to perform its intended function. Following the machining operations, the three Chinese-origin bushings are positioned at designated mounting locations and press-fit into the steering knuckle body using a hydraulic press. The completed assembly is then inspected and packaged for shipment.

input.facts: In your submission dated June 22, 2026, you requested a country of origin ruling for purposes of Section 301 duties, other tariffs and marking. Pictures and descriptions of the manufacturing processes were included in your submission. The item under consideration is identified as a Pick & Hook Set, SKU# 48-22-9215. The set consists of four tools, each with a metal shaft with a specially shaped tip attached to a plastic handle. These hand-operated tools are used for manual mechanical work, mainly to remove, pull, or position small parts such as O-rings, seals, clips, springs, and similar components in tight spaces. The user selects a hook or pick-shaped tool, inserts the tip into or around the part, and applies manual force through the handle to move or remove the component. The manufacturing process for each tool is identical. It begins in Thailand, where Chinese-origin steel coil is straightened to ensure uniform flatness and is cut to the required lengths of the shaft. The cut steel piece undergoes precision machining operations to form the functional geometry of the tool shaft. This includes shaping one end of the shaft into a specific hook, angle, or pick profile that is required for functional engagement with components. The shaft is further knurled to create textured patterns in order to improve grip retention and prevent slipping during use. The other end of the shaft is mechanically pressed to form the side wings that will attach to the plastic handle. The working end of the shaft is subsequently bent to the specific angle (e.g., 45°, 90°) to enable access into confined or obstructed spaces. The shaft is further shaped to ensure uniform diameter transitions and ergonomic geometry. The shaft is then sent to China where it is heat treated, electroplated, and assembled with a Chinese-origin injection-molded plastic handle.

In your letter dated June 7, 2026, on behalf of your client, Chervon North America, Inc., you requested a country of origin ruling on a paint sprayer. Descriptive literature was provided for our review. The item under consideration is described as a paint sprayer, which is a high-volume, low-pressure (HVLP) handheld electric sprayer designed to atomize low-viscosity liquids into a fine mist for finishing applications. The sprayer is intended for spraying interior and exterior walls, floors, furniture, wooden products, railings, doors, windows, cabinets, tables, chairs, and other small to medium-sized areas commonly encountered in residential and light commercial finishing work. In operation, the motor generates air pressure where a portion enters the tank through the intake pipe forcing the liquid through the siphon tube to the nozzle. Simultaneously, another portion of the air pressure atomizes the liquid exiting the nozzle into a fine mist for application. The paint sprayer itself consists principally of an ergonomic plastic handle and motor housing, an on/off switch and switch lever assembly, a paint container with internal suction tube, a flow control knob, a tip collar, an air cap, a set of interchangeable nozzles (1.3 mm, 1.5 mm, 2.0 mm, and 2.5 mm sizes), a spray width control lever, a filter and filter housing, an air tube and check valve assembly, and a brushless motor and printed circuit board assembly (motor/PCBA) housed within the motor enclosure. The product has a maximum flow rate of 833 ml/min (28 oz/min) and a paint container capacity of 1,200 ml (40 fl. oz.). The 24V 2.0 Ah lithium-ion battery pack is a removable rechargeable battery designed for use with the sprayer and other compatible Kobalt 24V cordless tools. The battery pack incorporates protection circuitry that guards against extreme temperature, over-discharge, and overcharge conditions, and features a four-LED power indicator that displays the remaining state of charge. The compatible battery charger is an AC-powered charging station that recharges a fully discharged 2.0 Ah battery pack in approximately 85 minutes. The battery pack and charger are designed to interlock with the bare tool and with each other through specified raised ribs and slots, ensuring proper electrical contact during use and during charging. 

Components and subassemblies for the paint sprayer kits are sourced from Thailand, Vietnam, China, and Malaysia, with final integration occurring in Thailand. The most critical subassembly, the brushless motor and printed circuit board assembly (PCBA), is manufactured in Vietnam. The Vietnamese operations for the motor/PCBA assembly encompass a comprehensive process, including automated press-fitting of balance rings and bearings onto the rotor shaft, automated adhesive dispensing and magnet installation, and dynamic balance testing with material removal for out-of-tolerance rotors. This is followed by machine winding of enameled wire onto stator laminations, terminal crimping, and stator testing via a diagnostic instrument. Further steps involve adhesive bonding and press-fitting of the stator into the motor housing, installation of the bracket, volute case supplement, impeller, fan cover, and sealing ring. An adhesive bead is then applied, and the rear cover is installed, leading to motor break-in and thermal curing. The process concludes with the soldering of brushless motor phase wires to the PCBA pads, locked-rotor and power-on testing, performance testing, visual inspection of solder joints, application of dustproof pieces and labels, and finally, the packing of the finished motor/PCBA assembly for shipment. Additionally, the battery charger is also produced in Vietnam, while the battery itself is manufactured in Malaysia. Other components used in the sprayer are sourced predominantly from China and Thailand. Components made in China include the gun set assembly hardware (nuts, air cap, 2.0 mm nozzle, adjust knob, gun set, O-rings, compressed spring, tube, connector, valve, suction tube, and seal), cylindrical pin, buckle, push rod, pressure spring, motor support, motor sealing ring, screws, switch, battery clip, air filter, additional cleaning accessories, the 2.5 mm and 1.5 mm nozzles, and a stripe label. Components made in Thailand include the regulator knob, the paint tank, the main housing assembly, the air inlet cover, the 1.3 mm nozzle, the retail bag, and the printed packaging carton. Thai-made plastic parts are produced in Thailand through injection molding and blow molding of plastic resins. The Vietnam-origin motor/PCBA assembly is subsequently imported into Thailand, where it is integrated with the housing, gun set assembly, paint container and suction system, air inlet components, switch, controls, fasteners, and other functional and structural parts to produce the completed paint sprayer. The processing operations performed in Thailand include the assembly of the motor/PCBA into the housing using tooling fixtures, followed by performance testing of the resulting subassembly, along with the air filter and air inlet cover. Additional flow-control and structural components are then assembled, including the gun mount component, which undergoes rotational and water spray testing. The final stages involve labeling, charging the battery, placing the sprayer, battery, charger, and accessories into the printed color box, and outer carton packing.

The product under consideration is described as aluminum laminated film intended for use with lithium-ion battery cells. You indicate that the aluminum laminated film prevents electrolyte leakage and is engineered to withstand high-pressure manufacturing while maintaining extreme formability and dimensional accuracy. The product consists of an outer layer of nylon/polyethylene terephthalate (PET) measuring 37 microns (0.037 mm) in thickness, a core layer of aluminum foil measuring 60 microns (0.06 mm) in thickness, and an inner layer of cast polypropylene (CPP) film measuring 80 microns (0.08 mm) in thickness. According to your submission, nylon/PET film of Chinese origin and an adhesive of Korean origin are sent to Thailand and made into the final product. In Thailand, the nylon/PET film are dry laminated together and then laminated to the aluminum foil that originates in Thailand by means of the adhesive. Next, the CPP film, which also originates in Thailand, is dry laminated to the foil. Finally, a slip agent coating is applied to improve the surface properties and handling of the film. The nylon/PET layer structurally supports the product and prevents tearing during deep drawing, the aluminum foil provides the primary moisture and gas barrier to ensure a hermetic seal, and the CPP layer provides electrolyte resistance and creates the final heat seal.

The merchandise under consideration is described as five models of fiber optic patch cord assemblies, identified by part numbers HGGQWQWTM, HGGQYQYTM, LAJGQYQWTM, LUJGQYQYTM, and CX1A0008R6B30. The subject assemblies are further described as fiber optic cables consisting of a fiber optic core, made of 144 fibers or 8 fibers, depending on the model number. The fiber core is enclosed within a jacket, and the cable assembly is terminated at each end with a fiber optic connector. The subject cables are used within various telecommunications industries to transfer optical data signals. In your request, you state the manufacturing process begins with the creation of optical fibers in the United States. This process begins with the melting and stretching of the glass raw material into a glass bar. This bar is then ground and cleaned before it is further stretched and drawn into the appropriate length and diameter for the individual optic fiber. This fiber is then coated with protective polymer, trimmed at the ends, and tested for strength and function before it is exported to China or Vietnam. In China or Vietnam, the fiber core is colored, tested, and jacketed with plastic and aramid yarn. The cable is then cut to length, and the ends are then prepared for the addition of the connectors. The connectors, originating in China, India, Japan, or the United States, are then assembled onto the ends in China or Vietnam, and the finished cable is inspected, tested and packaged for shipment to the U.S.

In your letter dated June 12, 2026, you requested a country of origin ruling on fiber optic cables. The merchandise under consideration is described as fiber optic patch cord assemblies, identified by individual model numbers 16FMTPLCOM4, 16FMTPLCSMF, 8FMTPLCOM4, and 8FMTPLCSMF. The subject assemblies are further described as multi-core fiber optic cables consisting of a fiber optic core, made of either 8 or 16 fibers which are either single-mode or multi-mode type depending on the model number. The subject cables are typically used for cabling in cabinets and systems with limited space and high cable management requirements within various telecommunications industries to transfer optical data signals. In your request, you detail two different manufacturing scenarios for all four models of fiber optic cables. In both scenarios, the optical fibers are sent to Vietnam where the fibers are colored, then jacketed with Chinese origin PVC or LSZH material and aramid yarn, and connectors from the United States are added to both ends of the cables. For certain models, Chinese origin branching kits or pull tabs are added depending on the customer’s needs. The finished fiber optic patch cord assemblies are then tested and packaged for export to the United States. In scenario 1, the optical fibers are sourced from a manufacturer in the United States where the optical fibers are drawn from the preform made in the United States. The finished optical fibers are shipped to Vietnam for further processing. In scenario 2, the optical fibers are drawn from a manufacturer in India where the preform is sourced from the United States. The finished optical fibers are shipped to Vietnam for further processing. 

We note that in both scenarios, the preforms are made by the same manufacturer in the United States by depositing silica particles onto a base rod or substrate tube, gradually forming the preform. Then, other elements are added to adjust the refractive index, forming the core and cladding structure. The process for drawing the optical fibers from the preforms is the same for both scenarios.

In your letter dated September 4, 2026, you requested a country of origin ruling on pressure washer nozzles and a sewer jetter kit. Descriptive literature was provided for our review. The first item under consideration is described as a 3-piece sewer jetter nozzle set (SKU T01-N02K). The item is packaged together as a set for retail sale and is designed exclusively for mechanical attachment to high-pressure hydro-jetting equipment or pressure washer hoses to clean, clear, and flush commercial and residential drainpipes. The nozzles are made of corrosion-resistant stainless-steel and contain three distinct spray nozzles designed to direct high-pressure fluid streams. The first is a rotating nozzle featuring an internal spinning mechanism driven by water flow to provide 360-degree scouring action against grease and roots. The second is a button nose nozzle with rear-facing thrust orifices designed to propel the hose forward while flushing loose debris. The third is a pointed jetter nozzle (also referred to as a penetrating or chisel nozzle) configured with a sharp profile and a forward-facing jet to punch through tough blockages and obstructions. The second item under consideration is described as a sewer jetter kit (SKU W02-P02K). The retail-packaged assortment is designed to convert a standard mechanical gas or electric pressure washer into a high-pressure pipe and drain cleaning system. The kit contains a high-pressure thermoplastic hose measuring 1/4-inch in internal diameter, reinforced with dual-layer high-tenacity terylene textile braiding and jacketed in weather and abrasion-resistant polyvinyl chloride (PVC). The hose is terminated at both ends with 1/4-inch Male National Pipe Thread (M-NPT) brass or stainless-steel fittings and possesses a rated maximum working pressure of 5,800 PSI and a burst pressure of 11,000 PSI. Imported alongside and packaged with the hose are several interchangeable hydro-jetter nozzles, including a stainless-steel button-nose nozzle and a brass rotating nozzle. The assortment further incorporates an M22
female-to-1/4-inch NPT female coupler, a 1/4-inch quick-disconnect plug for attachment to a pressure washer spray gun, a roll of polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) thread seal tape, two specialized open-ended spanners for fitting installation, and a set of cleaning pins for clearing nozzle orifice obstructions. The components are put up together in a single package for retail sale and function in an interdependent manner to project, disperse, and spray high-velocity water under pressure for the maintenance and cleaning of conduits. The nozzles, hose and adapters are made from components sourced from China and Malaysia. The Chinese components include the stainless-steel (for the nozzle washer, nozzle body, button nose nozzle, pointed nozzle, and fittings), screws, washers, O-rings, PVC plastic pellets for the hose, crimp sleeve, crimp sleeve, springs, retaining ring, and locking balls. The Malaysian components include the brass bar stock used for the nozzle rotating sleeve, female thread bushing, connector, coupler body, and locking sleeve. The plastic pellets are also imported from Malaysia to make the anti-slip sleeve. All of the components are then sent to Malaysia where the metal components are constructed by CNC machining the stainless-steel or brass depending on the component, precision drilling the parts, deburring and inspecting. Once the metal components are made, they are then assembled with the remaining Chinese components to form the complete nozzles and fittings. The hose is made by melting the white PVC plastic pellets and extruding the inner tube. Next, the reinforcing cord is wound around the outer surface of the inner tube to provide support and reinforcement. Then, the black PVC pellets are then extruded over the reinforcing cord to form the outer layer of the hose. The metal pieces are then added to the end of the hose using a crimping machine. All of the nozzles from item one are then tested and packaged in a white retail box. All of the items from item two are then tested and packaged in a brown retail box.

In your letter dated June 18, 2026, you requested a country of origin ruling on a flooring cutter. Product information was submitted with your request. The item under consideration is a 13-inch manually operated multi-flooring cutter (Model GS10104). As described, the item is a tool specially designed to cut various flooring panels using a lever-driven shearing action. The cutter is intended to be used for residential flooring installation, renovation, and do-it-yourself construction projects. During use, a flooring panel is positioned on the base plate and inserted between the blade (held by the blade holder) and the blade base. Once the panel is positioned, the user grips a handle at the end of a lengthy lever arm and pushes down, delivering the requisite mechanical force that actuates the downward motion of the blade to cut the flooring panel. You indicate it will be capable of cutting flooring materials of varying thickness such as laminate, engineered wood, fiber cement, and luxury vinyl tile and plank. Based on the submitted material, the flooring cutter features a base plate with feet and is designed to be placed on a flat surface during use. Furthermore, it will be imported as a standalone, manually operated tool without electric power or motor. Your submission suggests that the flooring cutter consists of four primary components: a steel blade, an aluminum blade holder, an aluminum blade base, and an aluminum lever handle. Additionally, 20 Chinese-origin components will be incorporated during final assembly processes in China to produce the finished flooring cutter. These Chinese components include, but are not limited to, a connecting rod, a guide rail, a rotary shaft, a limit block, an angle rod, a plastic base, and an aluminum support rod. For country of origin and marking purposes, you present three scenarios in which all components will be manufactured in Vietnam or China. In scenario one, steel from China or other countries is shipped to Vietnam where it undergoes blanking and preliminary edge grinding to produce a blade blank to the approximate size and shape of the finished blade. Similarly, aluminum raw materials are shipped to Vietnam 

where they undergo cutting to the size and shape of the blade holder. The blade holder blanks are then Computer Numerical Control (CNC) machined (e.g., drilling and milling) in Vietnam to produce the finished blade holder. In China, the blade blanks from Vietnam undergo heat treatment, hole punching, and additional edge grinding to produce the finished blade. Also in China, aluminum from China or other countries is cut to the approximate sizes and shapes of the blade base and lever handle and CNC machined to produce finished parts. Following that, the blade (blanked in Vietnam), blade holder (Vietnam), blade base (China), and lever handle (China) are assembled with 20 Chinese components by press fitting and fastening to produce the finished flooring cutter. Scenario two is the same as scenario one, except the blade base will also be manufactured in Vietnam. In scenario three, the blade blank, blade holder, blade base, and lever handle will all be manufactured in Vietnam.

In your letter dated August 10, 2026, you requested a country of origin ruling on a constant velocity joint subassembly. The merchandise under consideration is a spherical-type constant velocity (“CV”) joint sub-assembly (Product No. 8107156), designed for incorporation into an automotive drive shaft. The subassembly consists of an outer race, inner race, cage, and balls, all constructed of carbon steel. The subject CV joint subassembly measures approximately 163.6 mm by 106 mm by 106 mm and weighs approximately 2.166 kilograms. A drive shaft transfers rotational force from the vehicle’s transmission to the drive wheels. The subject CV joint subassembly is incorporated into the drive shaft and allows rotational force to be transmitted at a constant angular velocity while accommodating changes in the angle of the drive shaft resulting from steering and suspension movement. The outer and inner races contain precision raceways, or ball tracks, along which the balls travel. The cage maintains and guides the balls at specified intervals. You state that the raceways formed in the outer and inner races are critical to the function and performance of the CV joint because they determine the rolling paths of the balls and significantly affect the transmission of rotational force. You propose two manufacturing scenarios. Scenario 1 Under scenario 1, the outer race begins as a carbon-steel round bar of Chinese origin. The round bar is exported to the Republic of Korea, where it undergoes cutting and heat treatment followed by hot forging, which forms the material into the required general shape of the outer race. Following forging, the outer race undergoes shot blasting and turning. A rolling operation forms the spline and ring groove on the shank. The outer race then undergoes ball-grove rough and finish machining, during which the precision raceways, or ball tracks, are formed through cutting operations. Additional heat treatment is performed to achieve the
required final hardness and wear resistance. Internal and external-diameter grinding establishes the final dimensional and geometric accuracy of the article, while ball-groove grinding achieves the final shape and surface accuracy of the raceways. The outer race is subsequently painted, cleaned, and inspected in Korea. The inner race is manufactured in China from Chinese-origin material. The cage and balls are manufactured in the Republic of Korea from Korean-origin material. The finished outer race, inner race, cage and balls are assembled in the Republic Korea to form the subject CV joint subassembly. The completed subassembly is inspected in Korea for rotational performance, operating angle, assembly condition, and other functional and quality requirements. Scenario 2 Under scenario 2, the manufacturing process differs with respect to the initial production of the outer race. A carbon-steel round bar of Chinese origin undergoes cutting and heating treatment in China. The material is then warm forged and cold sized in China to form the general shape of the outer race. The resulting semi-finished outer-race forging is exported to the Republic of Korea. In Korea, the semi-finished forging undergoes shot blasting and turning to further machine the article into the required product shape. Rolling operations form the spline and ring groove on the shank. Ball-groove rough and finish machining is then performed in Korea to form the precision raceways, or ball tracks, through cutting operations. The outer race subsequently undergoes heat treatment in Korea to achieve the required final hardness and wear resistance. Inter and external-diameter grinding establishes the final dimensional and geometric accuracy of the article. Ball-groove grinding is then performed to achieve the final shape and surface accuracy of the raceways. The outer race is subsequently painted, cleaned, and inspected in Korea. As in Scenario 1, the inner race is manufactured in China, while the cage and balls are manufactured in the Republic of Korea. The components are assembled in Korea to form the subject CV joint subassembly, which is then inspected for rotational performance, operating angle, assembly condition, and other functional and quality requirements. In both scenarios, the spline is formed on the outer race in Korea.

In your letter dated August 27, 2026, you requested a country of origin ruling on an electric scooter, on behalf of your client Segway, Inc. The article under consideration is the Segway E2 Plus II electric scooter. The scooter consists of a steel frame to which various components are assembled, including a battery pack and battery box, an electric motor with integrated rear wheel, front wheel, controller, wiring harness, steering assembly, and front fork assembly. Your request presents two manufacturing scenarios for consideration. Under both scenarios, the scooter frame is manufactured in Vietnam from SPCC high-strength steel sheet and tubing sourced from Vietnam. With the exception of a drum brake pin sourced from China, the individual components comprising the frame are manufactured in Vietnam from steel sheet and tubing. In Vietnam, the steel sheet is first blanked using laser cutting equipment. The resulting blanks undergo various stamping, pressing, forming, machining, and tapping operations to manufacture the individual components of the scooter frame. These components include the left and right frame stampings, frame reinforcement plate, frame connecting plate, frame front support, fender mounting plate, kickstand fixing plate, name plate bracket and other components. The frame head tube is manufactured from tubing by laser cutting and computer numerical control (CNC) machining. After fabrication of the individual components, the components are transferred to the welding operation, where they are positioned in dedicated fixtures and permanently joined by robotic gas-shielded welding and other welding operations to form the completed scooter frame. Following welding, the frame undergoes finishing operations that include the removal of weld spatter, grinding, and smoothing of weld seams, correction of surface imperfections, alignment, and dimensional and structural inspection. You also provided video recordings depicting the manufacturing operations performed in Vietnam. The videos show the processing of steel material into the individual frame components and the subsequent welding and assembly operations used to manufacture the completed scooter frame.
Under Scenario 1, the completed frame undergoes electrodeposition coating (e-coating) in Vietnam before being exported to China. In China, the battery pack, battery box, electric motor with integrated rear wheel, front wheel, controller, wiring harness, steering assembly, front fork assembly, and other components are assembled to the Vietnamese-manufactured frame. The final assembly operations primarily consist of standard mechanical fastening and press-fit operations and take approximately 1.5 hours to complete. Under Scenario 2, the manufacturing and welding operations used to produce the completed frame are likewise performed in Vietnam. However, the completed frame is exported to China without undergoing e-coating. In China, the frame is e-coated before the remaining components are assembled to the frame in the same manner described above.

In your letter dated August 25, 2026, you requested a country of origin ruling on wheel hub bearing assemblies on behalf of Iljin Global Co., Ltd. The merchandise under consideration consists of wheel hub bearing assemblies, identified as Part Numbers IJ123161, IJ113067, IJ123124, IJ223089, and IJ223153. The assemblies are designed for use in motor vehicles and function as the interface between the rotating and non-rotating components of the vehicle’s suspension system. The principal components include a hub, outer ring, inner ring, rollers, cage, seals, hub bolt, and grease. The submission proposes two manufacturing scenarios. Scenario 1 Under Scenario 1, the hub, outer ring, and inner ring are manufactured in China from steel round bar. In China, the hub outer ring undergoes cutting, forging, rough turning, heat treatment, finish turning, drilling, and tapping, as applicable. The inner ring similarly undergoes forging, turning, and heat treatment. At the time these components are exported from China, they have been formed into dedicated hub and bearing-ring components but have not yet undergone precision grinding or super-finishing. The remaining components, including the rollers, cage, open seal, pack seal, encoder seal, hub bolt, and grease, are also of Chinese origin. In South Korea, the hub outer ring, and inner ring undergo precision grinding to form the raceways and achieve the required dimensional tolerances, followed by super-finishing to obtain the required roundness and surface roughness. The components are then washed and inspected. Final assembly also occurs in South Korea. The assembly operations include pressing the hub bolt into the hub, assembling the roller and cage components, machining and pressing the inner ring, orbital forming, installing the outboard seal, performing ABS output inspection, and conducting precision clearance matching. The completed assemblies are subsequently inspected, packaged, and shipped.
Scenario 2 The processing of the hub, outer ring, and inner ring under Scenario 2 is substantially the same as the processing described in Scenario 1. These components are manufactured in China through forging, turning, heat treatment, and other machining operations before being exported to South Korea as semi-finished hub and bearing-ring components. In South Korea, the hub, outer ring, and inner ring undergo precision grinding and super-finishing, followed by washing, inspection, and final assembly. Unlike Scenario 1, the rollers, cage, open seal, pack seal, encoder seal, hub bolt, and grease used in Scenario 2 are manufactured in South Korea or purchased as South Korean-origin components. The final wheel hub bearing assembly is completed and inspected in South Korea.

In your letter dated May 4, 2026, you requested a country of origin ruling on behalf of your client, Aperion Technologies, for Octal Small Form Factor Pluggable transceiver modules. The items concerned are referred to as Octal Small Form Factor Pluggable (OSFP) transceiver modules, model numbers 800G OSFPDR8, 800G OSFP2xDR4, 800G OSFP2xFR4, 1.6T OSFP2xDR4, and 1.6T OSFP2xFR4. These transceiver modules will be mounted to each end of a length of fiber optic cable. The subject merchandise is a hot-pluggable module that plugs into network devices, such as switches in data centers. It is used to convert an electrical signal into an optical signal, and conversely an optical signal back into an electrical signal. These transceivers are designed for use in 800 Gigabit Ethernet links on up to 500m of single mode fiber. They are used for networking in the data communications sector to receive, convert, and transmit different signals. We agree that these OSFP transceiver modules are similar to the ones discussed in rulings N358465, dated February 27, 2026 and N352670, dated September 10, 2025. The main components of the OSFP transceiver are the printed circuit board assembly (PCBA), the optical subassembly (OSA), and the transceiver housing. Scenario 1 OSA (China-Origin): The OSA includes both a TOSA (transmit optical subassembly) and a ROSA (receive optical subassembly). The TOSA and ROSA are referred to as “Tx” and “Rx.” The Tx (transmitter) part of the OSA is responsible for converting the electrical signals into optical signals and transmitting these signals over the optical fiber strand in the FA (fiber array) connected to it. One laser 

diode unit generates and focuses a light beam into a SiPho (Silicon Photonic) integrated circuit. The photonic integrated circuit splits the light signal into four light beams and takes electrical signals from the main PCBA to modulate the four collected light beams. Then, four lights are launched into the optical fibers of the FA via the isolator focus optics. The light beams then travel to the receptacle connector and out of the optical transceiver. The Tx part of the OSA is manufactured in China and attached to the Malaysia origin PCBA in China. The Rx (receiver) part of the OSA is responsible for receiving the optical signals transmitted from the Tx part of the transceiver and converting them back to electrical signals so that the communication equipment can understand them. The Rx part of the OSA consists of an Rx block, four photodiodes, two single-layer capacitors, and a transimpedance amplifier. The Rx part of the OSA receives four light beams from optical fibers and sends them to four photodiodes. It is the photodiodes that convert the light signals into electrical signals which are then amplified by the transimpedance amplifier on the PCBA. The Rx part of OSA is manufactured in China and attached to the Malaysia origin PCBA in China. Main Board PCBA (Malaysia-origin) The Main Board PCBA contains approximately 560 electrical elements sourced from various countries of origin. The main electrical element on the PCBA is the digital signal processor (DSP) chip of U.S.-origin. This is the highest value item on the BOM and a critical component of the PCBA. The Main Board PCBA is the foundation of the transceiver and imparts its essence. Without the Main Board PCBA, the Tx part of the OSA cannot generate optical signals and the Rx part of the OSA cannot convert optical signals into electrical signals. The DSP provides for signal amplification, detection, regeneration, and reconditioning. The DSP works with the OSA and provides electrical driving signals for the OSA (both the Tx and Rx). The DSP signals the laser diode of the Tx side of the OSA to emit optical signals into the fiber array and out of the transceivers. The DSP also processes optical signals from the fiber array into the transceiver on the Rx side of the OSA. The signal is not readable by the OSA until it is formatted by the DSP chips. On the receiving side, when the optical transceiver receives a signal from the OSA and converts the optical signal to electrical signal, the electrical signal is not readable by the optical transceiver until it undergoes further processing from the DSP. The Main Board PCBA also contains an erasable programmable read-only memory chip (EPROM) that will be programmed in Malaysia to provide the required instructions to perform the transceiver function. The EPROM information is saved in the flash memory of the MCU IC (Accelink PCBA Part Number 20719401 on the BOM). More than three-fourths of the total components of the transceiver are on the Main Board PCBA. Manufacturing of the Main Board PCBA in Malaysia: Production in Malaysia includes the creation of the PCBA via surface mount technology (SMT). The PCBA consists of numerous components/elements from various countries of origin. The SMT process is a multistage process requiring different types of specialized machines. The SMT process for the PCBA is as follows: 1. Solder paste printing. 2. Solder paste inspection (SPI). 3. SMT by means of a pick-and-place machine is used to populate the board with approximately 560 dedicated PCBA components. 4. Solder reflow to permanently adhere the components to the board. 5. Optical inspection (AOI). 6. Automated 3D x-ray inspection. 7. Another round of the SMT subprocess, repeating all previous steps. 

8. Conformal coating in order to protect the PCBA and its components. The coating is then dried and baked. 9. Manual visual inspection via microscope. Once the PCBA is assembled, it is sent to China where the OSA is attached. Manufacturing Steps in China: Attaching the OSA to the PCBA 1. Receive PCBA from Malaysia. 2. Attach the SiPo, laser diode, and substrate onto PCBA. 3. Perform wire bonding. 4. Attach the isolator to the PCBA with epoxy curing. 5. Attach and align Lens 1 to the PCBA with epoxy curing. 6. Attach and align Lens 2 to the PCBA with epoxy curing. 7. Attach and align the Tx Fiber Array with epoxy curing. 8. Rx FA alignment and attach with epoxy curing. 9. Attach a cover to protect the OSA on PCBA. 10. Test and inspect the OSA-on-PCBA. The OSA-on-PCBA is then returned to Malaysia where it is assembled into the finished transceiver. Final Assembly in Malaysia: Once the OSA-on-PCBA arrives back in the Malaysia, thermal grease is added to the light source in order to ensure heat dissipation and a component for heat release is attached to the light source. Next, an OSA cover is attached to the OSA via a UV curing and baking process. Next, the fiber router is attached, which routes fibers between the Tx part of the OSA subassembly, the Rx part of OSA subassembly, and the fiber connectors. Lastly, thermal pads are attached to allow the entire optical transceiver to dissipate heat. Once the above manufacturing in Malaysia is completed, the mechanical housing is attached to the parts, the software is loaded, and the transceiver undergoes electrical and optical performance tuning, testing, and quality assurance. Scenario 2 The manufacturing process for scenario 2 is similar to those in scenario 1 in relation to the work done in China. The main difference between the two scenarios is the manufacturing process in regard to the Main Board PCBA. Main Board PCBA (U.S.-origin) The Main Board PCBA contains the digital signal processor (DSP) chip of U.S.-origin. This part is the highest value part on the BOM and a critical component of the PCBA. The Main Board PCBA is the foundation of the transceiver and imparts its essence. Without the Main Board PCBA, the Tx part of the OSA cannot generate optical signals and the Rx part of the OSA cannot convert optical signals into electrical signals. The DSP provides for signal amplification, detection, regeneration, and reconditioning. The DSP works with the OSA and provides electrical driving signals for the OSA (both the Tx and Rx). The 4 DSP signals the laser diode of the Tx side of the OSA to emit optical signals into the fiber array and out of the transceivers. The DSP also processes optical signals from the fiber array into the transceiver on the Rx side of the OSA. The signal is not readable by the OSA until it is formatted by the DSP chips. On the receiving side, when the optical transceiver receives a signal from the OSA and converts the optical signal to electrical signal, the electrical signal is not readable by the optical transceiver until it undergoes further processing from the DSP. 

The Main Board PCBA also contains an erasable programmable read-only memory chip (“EPROM”) that will be programmed in the U.S. to provide the required instructions to perform the transceiver function. The EPROM information is saved in the flash memory of the MCU IC (Accelink PCBA Part Number 20719401 on the BOM). In addition to the DSP chip and the EPROM, the PCBA consists of approximately 560 electrical components from various countries of origin. More than three-fourths of the total components of the transceiver are on the Main Board PCBA. Manufacturing of the Main Board PCBA in United States: Production in the U.S. includes the creation of the PCBA via surface mount technology (“SMT”). The PCBA consists of numerous components/elements from various countries of origin. The SMT process is a multistage process requiring different types of specialized machines. It takes 10.2 minutes to assembly the PCBA in a fully automated process using specialized equipment. The SMT process for the PCBA is as follows: 1. The printed circuit board will undergo solder paste printing. 2. The board will undergo an initial solder paste inspection (“SPI”). 3. The board’s solder side will be surface-mounted by means of a pick-and-place machine that populates the solder side of the board with its dedicated PCBA components. 4. The solder side will undergo solder reflow to permanently adhere the components to the board. 5. The PCBA will undergo automated optical inspection (“AOI”). 6. The PCBA will undergo an automated 3D x-ray inspection. 7. The PCBA will undergo another round of the SMT subprocess, repeating all previous steps. 8. The PCBA will then undergo conformal coating in order to protect the PCBA and its components from moisture, dust, or other forms of damage. The coating is then dried and baked. 9. The PCBA will undergo a manual visual inspection via microscope. Once the PCBA is assembled, it is sent to China where the OSA is attached

In your letter dated June 10, 2026, you requested a country of origin ruling on behalf of your client, Jereh Energy Equipment and Technologies Corporation. The articles at issue are referred to as plunger pumps, model numbers JR600, JR600N, JR600S, JR1000Q, JR1000QS, JR1600Q, JR2500QL, JR2500Q, JR2500HD, JR2800Q, JR2800HD, JR3500D, JR3500HD, JR4000HD, JR5000QPE, JR5000QPW, JR7000QPE and JR7000E. The pumps, which feature 3 or 5 cylinders, continuously operate at 5600 horsepower and provide a maximum output of up to 7000 horsepower. The reciprocating linear motion of the plunger causes the expansion and contraction of the sealed cavity in the fluid end, realizing the suction and discharge of liquid. The gearbox transmits power to the crankshaft and other components. The pump is used primarily in the oil exploration and development industry for oilfield exploitation, oil and gas field fracturing, and high-pressure fluid transportation. With respect to origin, two scenarios detail the final assembly of the plunger pump in the United Arab Emirates (UAE). In both scenarios, a fluid end subassembly and seven additional subassemblies are produced in the UAE and joined together. In the first scenario, these seven subassemblies are manufactured using raw materials from China. In the second scenario, the seven subassemblies are produced using raw materials from China, South Korea, and Turkey. For the crankcase subassembly, oil holes undergo grinding and polishing processes to remove iron filings, burrs and flash. Bearings are disassembled and cleaned. Afterwards, the oil circuits are ground, polished, cleaned, and the plugs are tightened. A bearing retainer plate is then affixed to the lower end face of a bearing component, which is heated. Once cooled, the assembly is fixed with the bearing retainer plate. Afterwards, cooled cylindrical pins are placed into the crankshaft. The upper and lower parts of a connecting rod assembly are mounted onto the crankshaft using positioning pins, and an adapter plate is installed on the lower connecting rod and secured in place using screws. A data cable and protective spring of a temperature sensor are compressed and press-fit into the connecting rod seat assembly. Subsequently, outer rings of a 

bearing are cooled, installed onto the numbered crankcase bearing seats in sequence and fastened to outer rings with bolts. Bearing stoppers are installed using lock nuts and the outer ring of a bearing is interfaced onto the designated bearing seat and secured in place. Afterwards, a valve box is bolted to the crankcase, and the bores are machined to final dimensions. Using a press-fitting process, the end bearing shells are assembled onto the cast crosshead body. For the crosshead housing subassembly, lifting lugs are assembled onto a crosshead housing, which is followed by the installation of cylindrical pins into the pin holes of a crosshead sliding sleeve. Afterwards, end bearing shells are press-fit onto the cast crosshead body, and a connecting rod bushing is installed into the pin hole of the connecting rod shank. Next, a crosshead pin is installed into the crosshead component and connecting rod small-end bushing. Lastly, a data wire hole of the pony rod is aligned, and a data wire is fastened in place. As these steps are completed, the crosshead housing assembly is joined to the crankcase assembly. For the spacer subassembly, an O-ring and lip seal are installed into the outer sealing grooves of a pony rod oil seal cover. An oil seal baffle is then fastened onto the pony rod oil seal cover. The resulting assembly is bolted onto a spacer, and a crankshaft rotary joint is inserted into the central hole on the non-drive side of the crankshaft. In the next step, greased cylindrical pins are installed into the locating pin holes. And a crosshead box assembly is mounted onto the crankcase and bolted in place. The crosshead assembly is aligned to the studs at the upper part of the connecting rod, and a spacer is installed onto the crosshead housing assembly. The resulting assembly is screwed to the crosshead housing assembly, and the pony rod oil seal is assembled onto the spacer assembly and bolted in place. A fluid end subassembly is mounted onto the spacer assembly, and the resulting process is inspected, ensuring firm mating between fluid end, crankcase, crosshead housing and spacer assembly. Symmetrical multi-stage tightening is completed. For the gearbox subassembly, O-rings are installed into the grooves sequentially and an oil return baffle is secured in place. A gearbox assembly is secured to the crankcase assembly using lock washers and hex nuts, and a bearing retainer plate is secured onto the bearing housing on the drive side of the crankcase. Lastly, a level dial indicator is mounted. The completed gearbox assembly is then installed into the assembly that includes the previously joined subassemblies. For the suction subassembly, an end plug is screwed into the tail groove, which is followed by the installation of a pipe fitting. The pipe fitting is interfaced with the manifold and afterwards an O-ring is installed. The manifold is then positioned onto the fluid end assembly using washers and screwed in place. Afterwards, the subassemblies joined in the previous steps are appropriately fastened. Primer is applied to the mating surfaces, and the process continues by mounting and fastening a complete pump onto a base assembly. Once complete, a fixing block is embedded into a limit block, which is afterwards installed onto an end plate. Large washers, plain washers, and hex nuts are then installed in sequence and tightened. During the next step, a rubber scraper assembly is installed onto a scraper bracket and screwed in place. Connectors and barbed fittings are installed into the corresponding ports of the manual ball valve, which is subsequently installed into the oil pan welding assembly. The process continues by screwing a handle onto the oil pan assembly. Each completed pump is subjected to testing and is packaged for importation. It is mentioned that lubricant, grease and anti-seize compound are applied throughout the assembly process.

input.facts: In your letter dated August 12, 2026, you requested a country of origin ruling on behalf of your client, SEI Optifrontier Vietnam, Ltd. The merchandise under consideration is described as optical fiber cables, identified by their individual model numbers AN003870 (Model 1), AN003871 (Model 2), and AN003920 (Model 3). Models 1 and 2 are further described as in-rack fan-out (IRFO) cables, which allow a multi-fiber cable to be split at the optical fiber endpoints into individual connections. Model 3 is further described as a multi-drop (MD) cable, which is a single cable with optical fibers that are branched out along a cable route to serve multiple locations or devices along its path. All three models are for use within various telecommunications industries to transfer optical data signals. In your request, you state that the manufacturing process for all three optical fiber cable models begins in Japan with the production of the glass preform. This preform is heated and drawn into thin optical fiber strands with precise diameter and transmission characteristics. Protective and reinforcing materials, such as aramid yarn and flame-retardant PVC, are then applied to the fiber. Prior to export to Vietnam, Model 3 undergoes additional processing in Japan. Multiple cords are stranded—twisted together and secured with plastic tape—to create a bundled cable configuration. This is followed by a jacketing process, where an additional outer protective PVC layer is extruded over the stranded cords. This creates the integrated cable structure required for the MD configuration, providing enhanced mechanical protection and environmental resistance. In Vietnam, the cables are cut to the required lengths. The fiber ends are then processed, grouped in the required order, stripped, and inserted into the ferrule using adhesive. The ferrule and fiber then undergo polishing and surface inspection to ensure compliance with shape specifications and visual standards. Finally, connectors are assembled and secured to the cord via crimping and heating at both ends. The finished product is then bagged and packed into cartons or reels for export to the United States.

It consists of twomain components, identified in your submission as a body assembly and a frame. The body assemblytransforms hydraulic energy into mechanical impact force. Afterwards, theframe is shot blasted, deburred, and subjected to other mechanical finishing operations. The body assembly issourced from China as a finished assembly.Additional components are sourced domestically in Korea, including a cap, a wear plate, and upper and lowercushions, which are described as molded plastic components that support the body assembly inside the frame.The cap is a mounting bracket for connecting the breaker to the excavator arm. The wear plate is installedinside the frame to support the body and reduce wear.Final assembly occurs in South Korea and begins with inspecting, testing, and painting the Chinese bodyassembly. Afterwards, the lower cushion, the Chinese body assembly, the upper cushion, and the wear plateare inserted inside the frame. The cap is secured to the top of the frame using hex bolts and washers, whichare then torqued to specification. Lastly, the breaker is cleaned with compressed air, painted, and packagedwith a rod, which is the working tool that directly strikes the material.
